title: Greg Jensen - Co-CIO of Bridgewater   Podcast   In Good Company   Norges Bank Investment Management

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Greg Jensen - Co-CIO of Bridgewater   Podcast   In Good Company   Norges Bank Investment Management.docx

speakers: interviewer (Norges Bank Investment Management podcast host)
summary: NBIM podcast with Bridgewater co-CIO Greg Jensen (Nov 2025). Argues modern mercantilism, the AI capex boom and record US capital concentration are the three themes; mercantilism and military spending are inflationary, fiscal limits make bonds a weaker diversifier. Advocates global diversification and survival across scenarios; describes Bridgewater's compounded-knowledge and AI-agent process.

completeness_estimate: 0.86 - first reader captured the macro themes, fiscal-limits and portfolio views well; missed the AI J-curve, the US growth forecast, divided-Fed and institutions points, the case for bonds at higher real yields, the systematise-then-focus-on-gaps method and the Spanish-flu analogy caveat

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: the three big themes that I'm concerned about or focused on are a the change in how the global and US economy uh is being managed
claims.claim: Three macro themes: a shift to modern mercantilism (reaction to China's rise), the AI technology revolution, and record concentration of capital in US equities and illiquid assets.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: capital is more concentrated in the US than ever, more concentrated in equity and illquid assets. Um so a kind of risky setup.
claims.claim: Capital concentration in US assets is a risk factor, so understanding where money has flowed, why, and how likely it is to reverse matters.
claims.indicator: global capital allocation to US assets
claims.testable: partly - foreign holdings of US assets data

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: a major change in the 1980s, a shift towards small government, a lot of capitalism
claims.claim: Regime shift analogy: the 1980s turn to small government and free markets is now being replaced by mercantilism (tariffs, state control, trade as zero-sum), so investors must adapt rather than assume the old economy.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: You would have thought that people would have taken down their massive risk concentration in the US because it's changing so quickly.
claims.claim: Expected effect of mercantilism: a higher risk premium on US assets and diversification away from the US; muted at the index level because AI offsets.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: the worst performance of US equities relative to the rest of the world equities in common currency terms that you've had over that 15-ear period
claims.claim: Under calm index averages, US equities posted their worst relative performance vs the world in 15 years, so averages hide stress visible in sub-components (US ex-AI, gold).
claims.indicator: US vs world equity relative return in common currency; gold

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: everything looks fine on the surface. If you look underneath that, split up the equity market.
claims.claim: Look beneath index averages (e.g. S&P ex-AI names, gold) to see shifts the headline averages hide.
claims.indicator: S&P 500 ex-AI vs rest of world; gold

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: take all of your human intuition, translate that into um algorithms
claims.claim: Bridgewater's method: write down beliefs, stress-test them, and encode human intuition into algorithms (an expert system).

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: when will machines write the rules not just support the rules which we've been doing
claims.claim: Bridgewater built an AI agent investor (started 2022, producing alpha by 2024) run as a separate entity to generate independent ideas; machines learning rules rather than copying human intuition.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: I used to say the bubble's ahead of us, not behind us.
claims.claim: AI: bubble is ahead, not behind - in the early phase people underestimated how much will be invested.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: It's not a capex cycle that's the same as other capex cycles. This money is going to get spent, right?
claims.claim: AI capex is driven by strategic, non-profit motives of firms whose businesses are threatened, so spending persists beyond normal ROI discipline.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: we are in a more dangerous phase
claims.claim: Current AI phase is a resource grab (power, chips, scientists) where compounding must continue in the physical world, a more dangerous but not bubble phase.
claims.indicator: AI capex; power and chip supply

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: the depreciation schedule is probably going to be quite fast
claims.claim: Risk: AI-generated efficiency gains will obsolete current chips and assets quickly (fast depreciation).

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: This is how they're going to get their revenue. Not at all. Nvidia can get as much revenue as it wants.
claims.claim: Vendor financing is not bubble-style demand creation but Nvidia building a controlled ecosystem versus Google's full stack, with scarce chips as leverage.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: I think less than a thousand.
claims.claim: Cutting-edge AI scientists number under a thousand, making talent the binding constraint; poaching slows scientific progress.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: The US is no longer the US
claims.claim: Mercantilist shift: US no longer pursues international cooperation as before; the rest of the world has not retaliated against tariffs (picked off one by one), but is showing home bias and domestic investment.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: the biggest collapse in support for the United States in the rest of the world that we've ever seen
claims.claim: Collapse in US goodwill drives populist, mercantilist politics (shift to populist right then left), with less international cooperation.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: Two big things, right? You get tariffs
claims.claim: Mercantilism is inflationary: tariffs and resilient supply chains replace cheapest sourcing, reversing 30 years of productivity gains.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: there's nothing more inflationary really than military spending
claims.claim: Military spending is especially inflationary because it creates demand for labour and goods with no supply into the real economy; Germany and Europe are surging fiscal and defense spending.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: growth is dominated by this AI investment AI investment while starting to take up power capacity and whatever is very low
claims.claim: AI investment gives growth with low labour intensity, so growth is concentrated while the labour market is weak and the effect is initially disinflationary; AI adds ~1pt of 2% US growth.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: we think the fed is very comfortable above two and a half and probably we're in the three range as a base right now
claims.claim: Base case: US inflation about 3% for the next couple of years with Fed tolerant above 2.5%, versus breakeven near 2.25-2.5%.

correction.issue: Breakeven number misstated: he said breakeven inflation is around 2.5%, not 2.25-2.5%.
correction.fix: Base case: US inflation around 3% for the next couple of years, with a Fed comfortable above 2.5%, versus breakeven inflation priced around 2.5%, with risk of higher.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: lowering real rates into a boom like this is particularly inflationary
claims.claim: Populist control of the central bank leading to lower real rates during an AI boom would be inflationary.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: we're all Brazil now
claims.claim: Fiscal-constraint thesis: developed economies (UK, soon US) are constrained like Brazil even with domestic currency debt; fiscal expansion in constrained countries lowers currency, equities and raises rates.
claims.direction: short gilts and currency of constrained countries; long unconstrained (Germany)

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: when you get constrained spending money becomes counterproductive rather than productive
claims.claim: Fiscal limits depend on domestic savings, productivity and willingness to hold your currency (Japan 300% debt vs Brazil 60-80%); beyond the limit, spending raises rates and hurts assets.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: how do we survive in the wide range of possible worlds rather than try to pick the best thing
claims.claim: Philosophy: survive across a wide range of worlds because compounding depends on avoiding bad outcomes.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: Most people have moved away from diversification because it hasn't worked for 15 years.
claims.claim: US-only equity concentration is a trap after 15 years of success; build a much more globally diversified portfolio.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: companies that directly compete between Europe and the US, they're generally priced cheap
claims.claim: Europe is investable: fiscal shift supports domestic profits, shareholder returns improved, and companies are cheaper than US peers with better earnings and management.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: the biggest risk of being invested in China is your government saying you can't be invested in China
claims.claim: China matters for diversification; its leadership moved to support the private sector and equity market to compete on AI; main risk is political access.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: All of a sudden the correlation between bonds and equities and currency will shift when you hit limits.
claims.claim: Bonds are no longer the 30-year diversifier because fiscal limits shift correlations, and fiscal policy responds to disinflation, so bonds do not hedge deflation as well.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: you're going to have this big competition for capital between fiscal and AI
claims.claim: Massive fiscal supply plus AI ecosystem spending (tech firms turning from net savers to spenders, private credit) creates a shortage of capital, pushing real rates up, opposed by US central bank pressure.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: this is not very helpful technology
claims.claim: Crypto: use cases mostly speculation, attracts corruption; Bitcoin has some merit as non-government money and gold substitute, but AI is a better bet.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: you have to do that by compounding understanding
claims.claim: Bridgewater's edge: understand the global financial system deeply and build portfolios, by writing down beliefs and compounding knowledge in human- and machine-readable form with a record of every change.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: If that knowledge is not in what we call our secure garden
claims.claim: Enforcement rule: research counts only when translated into compounded knowledge (plain-English reasoning plus code).

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: the reasoning is written and the manifestation of that reasoning in code exists and otherwise you get no credit for it
claims.claim: One common platform for all research in place of mixed tools makes research replicable and lets AI audit the rules.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: I wanted ya to be uncorrelated to pure alpha
claims.claim: AI venture run separately, designed around AI rather than humans, to avoid copying human flaws and get an uncorrelated alpha source; now being merged back.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: One of the reasons that AI hasn't swept through corporate America is people keep trying to replace humans with it
claims.claim: AI adoption works when processes are redesigned around the technology rather than replicating human tasks (Amazon robots example).

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: the reason we survived was partially this process that I'm saying is good and you make good decisions, but much more important is risk control
claims.claim: Survival over 50 years came mainly from risk control, accepting that all are flawed.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: we totally screwed it up because we were trying to systemize
claims.claim: COVID lesson: trying to systemise a unique shock made the model slow; Bridgewater now accelerates new research into positions before it is fully systematized and gives researchers independence (a controlled override).
claims.conditions: novel shocks with no systematic analogue

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: Barely but yes.
claims.claim: Overruling the system helps barely on average, so it is done rarely and with discipline.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: you have to know the future better than other people do in otherwise you should just be at the benchmark
claims.claim: Markets are a probabilistic game requiring being wrong often but right more; poker skills (incomplete information, probability, handling mistakes) transfer; machines surpassed humans in poker, an analogy for edge when machines learn faster than humans.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: you have to fight against certain human things
claims.claim: Radical transparency with feedback aimed up at leaders, and measuring that managers elicit criticism, lets best ideas win.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: The worst managers in the company are the ones that their people say all good things about.
claims.claim: Managers who get the most negative feedback are best, as it shows independent thinking is drawn out.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: I thought it would have bigger impact than it has as an example
claims.claim: Admission: the impact of mercantilism on markets has been smaller than he expected, partly explained by AI offset.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: being in unwilling to say what they believe or being unwilling to listen to other people
claims.claim: Hiring: balance open-mindedness and assertiveness; two failure modes are not speaking up and not listening.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: pain plus reflection equals progress
claims.claim: Ray Dalio's principle: reflect on pain to make progress; Dalio's succession took 15 years.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: we centralized the decision-m largely at the CIO level
claims.claim: Hardest decision: moving from CIO-centralised decisions to independent investors, requiring removal of long-tenured people from the process.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: all these investments have a Jc curve in the first [L340] phase you don't get you spend a lot of resources you don't get a lot of output other than the investment itself
claims.claim: AI investment follows a J-curve: in the first phase it absorbs large resources with little output beyond the investment itself, and only later becomes strongly disinflationary, so the disinflation is further out than many assume.
claims.testable: partly - capex share vs measured productivity over time

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: above potential two two and a like two and a half kind of percent growth and um and but a lot of that one and a half percent or so is going to be AI
claims.claim: Forecast: US growth next year a little above potential at about 2.5%, with roughly 1.5 points from AI investment, producing a two-track economy of a concentrated AI boom alongside a weak labour market.
claims.indicator: US real GDP growth, AI investment contribution
claims.direction: US growth above potential, labour weak
claims.conditions: AI capex continues; European fiscal push
claims.testable: yes - compare with realised GDP and investment contributions

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: for a while you're going to have this very divided Fed and where the chairman may be in the minority
claims.claim: View: a new Fed chair aligned with the administration may be outvoted often next year, giving a divided Fed until more aligned governors are appointed, a policy-uncertainty source.
claims.indicator: FOMC dissents / votes against the chair
claims.conditions: politically appointed chair with board not yet aligned
claims.testable: partly - dissent counts and rate volatility around FOMC

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: I think we're in this death march on institutions you've already seen that the World Trade Organization what does it even do now
claims.claim: International institutions (e.g. WTO) have lost their function and US domestic institutions are weakening fast, part of why the US is becoming a less exceptional, higher-risk-premium place to invest.
claims.direction: higher risk premium on US assets
claims.testable: no - institutional quality is hard to measure

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: interest rates have risen and real interest rates have risen such that there is a place for bonds in portfolios
claims.claim: After many investors left bonds at zero rates, the rise in nominal and real yields means bonds again deserve a place in portfolios, though with weaker diversification than in the past 30 years.
claims.conditions: starting yields well above zero; less useful where fiscal limits bind
claims.testable: yes - bond forward returns conditional on starting real yield

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: because that's all systemized they could just focus on what we're missing what is happening in the world today that you're worried that process doesn't have reflected
claims.claim: Research method: once accumulated understanding is fully systematised, the human research team (a couple hundred people) can concentrate only on what the systematic process does not yet capture, such as new regimes like modern mercantilism.

claims.speaker: Greg Jensen
claims.quote: we had done work on the 1917 Spanish flu, but the economic impact of the Spanish flu because it was so disperate was so different than what ended up happening and we knew it
claims.claim: Caveat on historical analogies: Bridgewater's systematic COVID response leaned on the Spanish flu precedent even though they knew its economic impact differed, so a known-imperfect analogue embedded in process can override better current knowledge.
